title: Senate cuts P19.8 billion budget for 2 ayuda programs
summary: The Senate has slashed P19.8 billion from two major cash aid programs to raise the subsidy for Philippine Health Insurance Corp. to P94.2 billion under the proposed national budget for next year,…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate has slashed P19.8 billion from two major cash aid programs to raise the subsidy for Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) to P94.2 billion under the proposed national budget for next year, Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito said yesterday.

In a chance interview with reporters before the start of plenary deliberations on the budget, Ejercito said the panel cut P9.9 billion each from the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations and the Medical Assistance Program, reallocating the funds to boost PhilHealth’s subsidy from the P73 billion approved in the House of Representatives’ General Appropriations Bill.

“The ayuda partly we will slash and place much of it in PhilHealth. Therefore, PhilHealth’s subsidy will increase by almost P20 billion,” he said. “We were targeting P100 billion, but the fiscal space is tight.”

Alongside a higher PhilHealth subsidy, Ejercito said the Senate increased funding for zero-balance billing, as well as for preventive care such as immunization and health promotion and for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program to upgrade provincial and locally funded hospitals.

He also said the Senate is pushing for a wrap-up of plenary debates by tomorrow so as to avoid a Saturday session, out of consideration for exhausted staff who had to work overtime from 1 p.m. Tuesday to 2 a.m. yesterday. The bicameral conference is tentatively set for Dec. 9 or 10.

Also yesterday, the Senate swiftly approved the budgets of the Office of the Ombudsman at P8.262 billion and the Commission on Elections at P29.163 billion. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla and Comelec Chairman George witnessed the chamber’s approval of their budgets.
Ping: P600 million wasted

Sen. Panfilo Lacson, meanwhile, revealed that roughly P600 million in public funds has been wasted on commitment fees and penalties for unimplemented foreign-assisted projects (FAPs), with the realigned allocations likely ending up in anomalous flood control projects.
In posts on X, Lacson blamed congressional realignments for stalling the projects, leaving taxpayers shouldering the penalties incurred.

“During our budget plenary debates last Monday, it was revealed that we already paid $1.5 million and $8 million in commitment fees and penalties because foreign-assisted projects were not implemented. This may be because Congress moved the funds elsewhere using its ‘power of the purse.’ Together, that’s about P600 million of public money wasted,” Lacson said.
“And worse, we have good reason to suspect, most probably, the realigned FAP funds went to some ghost and substandard flood control projects,” he added.
Ejercito disclosed during Monday’s budget deliberations that the government paid $1.5 million in commitment fees in 2024 and $8 million in 2025.

“Wasted. Is that good economic sense? Definitely not. And these are long-term, high-impact projects. Not implemented because Congress realigned the budget,” Lacson said, noting that there is still time for lawmakers to restore FAP allocations to their original National Expenditure Program (NEP) levels in the 2027 budget bill.

While the Senate restored the overall 2027 FAP allocation to P459.16 billion from the House’s P328.45 billion, Lacson noted that the chamber altered the funding mix – increasing unprogrammed support to P102.34 billion from the NEP’s P42.55 billion, while reducing loan proceeds to P223.41 billion (from P271.22 billion) as well as counterpart funds to P133.4 billion from P145.37 billion.
He cited the Laguna Lakeshore Road Network, whose P35.209-billion NEP allocation was cut by the House to P8.209 billion and only partially restored by the Senate to P22.209 billion.
Earlier, Lacson proposed an overhaul of the 2027 budget by scrapping P54 billion for multipurpose buildings (MPBs) and P85 billion in fragmented cash aid outside the 4Ps program.
His team has detected multiple appropriations for 30 MPBs and double funding for a Zamboanga flood control project.

“This is the time when Congress has to make some sacrifice. The ball is in our court. We must do our part,” he said. “Can we at least do our part for nation building, (for) economic growth instead of the usual more of the same misplaced priorities?”
Unfinished classrooms
During budget deliberations last Tuesday, it was revealed that only about 500 of the 18,950 classrooms targeted for 2026 have been completed and put to use.

Pressed by Sen. Imee Marcos on the status of the classroom-building program, DepEd budget sponsor Sen. Bam Aquino confirmed that while the rest are still undergoing construction or bidding, only a fraction has been turned over and opened to students.
Marcos expressed frustration over the sluggish pace despite last year’s record education allocation.

“What was allocated last year was so big, it was really a blockbuster last year, first time in history. Then there was finger-pointing, there was blame game. Huge money, and then nothing. Still, no classroom, why? That’s the question,” she said.

Aquino explained that of the P21.45 billion assigned to the Department of Public Works and Highways for 6,000 classrooms, only P7 billion has been transferred so far and only one of three lots has been subjected to bidding, with DPWH conducting its own validation on top of DepEd’s.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara thanked the Senate for approving the department’s P915.49- billion budget.

“We are deeply grateful to Sen. Bam Aquino and the entire Senate for keeping our learners front and center during these budget talks. Every peso we invest in basic education goes straight to where it matters most: safer classrooms, well-nourished kids and better equipment and resources for our teachers,” Angara said. — Bella Cariaso
